findings.title: Client sends a new request to the project email address
findings.expected: The message is classified, becomes a work item under the right engagement, and says how it got there.
findings.actual: Classified and filed under the mailbox's scope as OAPIL-004, at High severity — and the severity is reported as guessed rather than stated, because it came from the words "blocking" and "production" rather than from a rule. Rules that fired: Inventory to Priya. The record is created through the same reducer as a person's, so the transition graph, permissions and audit apply. It arrives as "Open": a machine may file work, it may not decide it is being worked on. An unknown address is refused: "No mailbox is configured for someone-else@axiocloud.example. Configuration → Routing & int"
findings.stops: at a real client message — the first mile now exists. A Logic App polls the configured mailbox every three minutes and the endpoint has been proven by a posted message that became an issue, so the two halves meet at the POST; no email a client actually sent has yet travelled the whole path. This becomes PASS when one has.
findings.impact: The gap changed shape today rather than closing. It was "no connector exists"; it is now "the connector is deployed and polling and nobody has watched a real message arrive" — a verification, not a build.

findings.title: The same message is delivered twice
findings.expected: The second delivery is recognised and does not create a second record.
findings.actual: The endpoint refuses a repeat on the sender's own message id and answers "already received" rather than an error — the caller did nothing wrong, and retrying is what it should do. It also refuses everything unless a shared secret is configured: an endpoint that creates records from the internet does not run open. Both are read from the route here rather than driven, because exercising them needs a live database.
findings.stops: at a live database — the logic is in the endpoint and cannot be driven by this harness
findings.impact: Duplicate delivery, which is the normal failure of every mail integration, does not produce duplicate work.

findings.title: Client replies on an existing issue
findings.expected: The reply is recorded against the issue, the issue stops looking stale, and the trail shows who said what and when.
findings.actual: Note recorded, authored by "Validator", and the issue's last activity moved to 2026-08-15.
findings.stops: before the reply arrives on its own — the note is typed by a consultant, not received
findings.impact: The record is right once someone transcribes it. Nothing guarantees they do.

findings.title: Client sends an ambiguous request
findings.expected: The system marks it as needing clarification, and the SLA clock stops while the client holds the ball — without the committed date ever moving.
findings.actual: Waiting shows Blocked; leaving after ten days banks pausedDays=10 with statusSince=2026-08-15; the committed date stays 2026-08-10; and on the 18th the health comparison shifted by the bank reads "On Track" where the naked one reads "Overdue". Nothing asks the client automatically — the reply is written from the record (phase 5), which is a person's act, not the clock's.

findings.title: Client sends an attachment
findings.expected: The file is stored, attached to the issue, and can be produced later as evidence.
findings.actual: The evidence record is still just a description (url: none) — and beside it there is now a Document, which exists only when bytes exist. An upload path exists: POST /api/documents stores the file in the firm’s SharePoint library through Graph and records what came back, in that order, so a crash leaves an orphaned object rather than a record pointing at nothing. GET /api/documents/[id] streams it back with a per-request check, and no storage URL is ever put in the page payload. What has not happened is a real file making the trip: the store needs an administrator to grant Files.ReadWrite.All and to name a drive, and until then every upload is refused at the door with that sentence.
findings.stops: at a consented document library. The model, the store contract, both endpoints and the screen are built and the not-configured refusal is the only path exercised — no file has yet been stored or produced. This becomes PASS when one has.
findings.impact: Evidence still cannot be produced at a governance meeting, but the reason has changed from "nothing was built" to "one consent has not been granted", which is a different and much smaller job.

findings.title: The same defect is reported twice
findings.expected: The duplicate is detected, linked to the original, and does not become a second stream of work.
findings.actual: The link and the Superseded status both work, closing sets actualEnd to 2026-08-15, and the transition graph makes the duplicate call an explained one — Superseded needs a reason, which is now on the trail. Detection is still manual: the duplicate-detection agent is a registry record with no runtime.
findings.stops: at detection — a person must notice
findings.impact: Duplicates are found late, after two people have worked the same fault.

findings.title: An issue needs another consultant to help
findings.expected: A contributor can be added without taking ownership, and the trail shows both.
findings.actual: The mechanism works: an unbounded responsibility holds 2 people, the owner is still Priya, and the change is audited. But the shipped operating model has 3 responsibilities — Owner, Accountable Party, Raised By — and 0 of them accept more than one name. Contributor is a type the firm must invent.
findings.stops: at the shipped model — helping is possible, but not offered
findings.impact: Out of the box, the only way to involve a second person is to hand over ownership.

findings.title: Work is assigned to someone who is not available
findings.expected: The system refuses, or warns, because that person is on leave or already committed.
findings.actual: Assignment now consults capacity through the same arithmetic `upsertAllocation` uses. A name that is in no directory comes back "unknown" rather than free — "“Someone Who Does Not Exist” is not in the people directory, so nothing can be checked abo" — which is the distinction that matters, because `capacityFor` would otherwise report seven and a half hours a day of somebody nobody has ever described. The seeded owner reads "unknown", an unowned issue "clear". Only absence refuses: being away for the whole window is a fact and is blocked, while being fully committed is a judgement and is recorded against the change instead. A refusal names the escape and `acceptUnavailable` takes it, so the decision is written down rather than worked around.
findings.stops: at the directory, which is still a free-text column rather than a reference
findings.impact: Work can no longer be handed to somebody who is away without that being a recorded decision. It can still be handed to a typo, because the owner column holds text and nothing constrains it to a person.

findings.title: A consultant is already overallocated
findings.expected: Committing more of their time surfaces the conflict before it is agreed, and the numbers behind it.
findings.actual: Refused with the arithmetic rather than a shrug: "Priya is committed to 86.4h against 57.6h available — 28.8h more than exists. Commit it anyway if that is the decision — it will be recorded as one." Committing it anyway is allowed and recorded as a decision — the trail says "Deliberately overallocated: Priya is committed to 86.4h against 57.6h available …". Booking a week of leave moves the same figures: available falls from 57.6h to 17.6h and the existing commitment becomes an overallocation. A four-day week is honoured, so nobody is assumed full-time.
findings.impact: A plan can now be checked against the people who have to deliver it, and deliberate overallocation is distinguishable from an accident.

findings.title: New work arrives and there is not enough capacity for it
findings.expected: The delivery plan is shown to be impossible before it is agreed.
findings.actual: The plan needs 90h and 36h have been committed to it — a shortfall of 54h, visible in week one rather than week six. 1 record has no estimate and is invisible to the figure, which is stated rather than treated as zero. The scheduled pass watches this condition too, so a plan that stops fitting is raised once rather than found in week six.
findings.impact: A delivery manager can see the gap, and the pass raises it once when it appears rather than leaving it to be found.

findings.title: An issue approaches its SLA target
findings.expected: It is flagged at risk before it breaches, and the person who can act is told.
findings.actual: Health computes as "At Risk" from dates and progress, and the scheduled pass turns it into an event: "Due 2026-08-16 and 0% complete with most of the window gone.". Going at-risk is not something anybody does — it is time passing against a date nobody moved — so it needed a clock rather than a channel, and a rule subscribes to it like any other event.
findings.impact: Work at risk reaches the person who can act, instead of waiting to be noticed by whoever happens to open the app.

findings.title: An issue breaches its SLA
findings.expected: It is overdue, somebody is told, and it appears on the report.
findings.actual: Health is "Overdue", the daily IMS lists it, and the pass tells the owner: "OAPIL-2 is overdue — Subject OAPIL-2. Due 2026-08-10, and 5 working days have passed.". The message is attributed to the scheduled pass rather than to a person, because a clock decided it.
findings.impact: A breach is routed to somebody rather than only reported to whoever opens the report.

findings.title: The pass runs every morning for a fortnight and nothing changes
findings.expected: The same condition is reported once, not fourteen times.
findings.actual: 1 message on the first run and 0 across the next thirteen: the condition is counted, not repeated — and the memory still records it as true, so the quiet is suppression rather than the condition having stopped being detected. Moving the date cleared it, and missing the new one raised it again — a date somebody moved and then missed is a different fact from the first miss.
findings.impact: This is the failure that makes scheduled alerting useless in its second month. The pass is built around avoiding it rather than patched to.

findings.title: The pass is switched on, and later a condition is added to what it watches
findings.expected: The first run says what is wrong now; a condition ticked later arrives quietly.
findings.actual: The first run raised 1 and seeded nothing — a firm switching the pass on is told what is wrong now, and a condition true at that moment would otherwise never be announced at all. Ticking staleness on later found 3 instances and raised none of them, because that one fires at seven the next morning into a stream people already trust. The run after that raised 0.
findings.impact: The two cases with no history are treated differently on purpose, and the difference is now pinned rather than described.

findings.title: The pass acts as a machine
findings.expected: What it does is attributed to the clock, and limited to what a machine may do.
findings.actual: The trail says "Scheduled pass" rather than a person's name, because nobody decided it. The pass holds ROLE_AUTOMATION — not the fallback role an unrecognised human would get — so it may file work and say things about it, and may not close anything ("Close work is not something Automation can do here.") or change the operating model ("Configure the platform is not something Automation can do here.").
findings.impact: An automated path cannot quietly acquire administrator rights by being nobody in particular.

findings.title: A project milestone becomes at risk
findings.expected: The milestone shows the risk, and it rolls up to the project so a governance meeting sees it.
findings.actual: A late issue rolls up: its process area now reports 2026-08-01 → 2026-08-09 with 17% complete. Milestones exist as a row kind, but no milestone record ties to a SOW or a payment.
findings.stops: at the milestone as a commercial object
findings.impact: Delivery risk is visible; contractual consequence is not.

findings.title: A consultant records time against an issue
findings.expected: The hours land on the work item, move it off stale, and become the actual half of the estimate.
findings.actual: 5.5h recorded across 2 activities — 3.5h billable, 2h not — and the issue is no longer stale (last activity 2026-08-15). Refused: a future day ("Time cannot be recorded for a day that has not happened."), an 18-hour entry, and 1.37 hours. Removing an entry withdraws it rather than destroying it.
findings.stops: at money — hours are recorded, and a rate to multiply them by does not exist anywhere
findings.impact: Actual effort, variance and utilisation now have a source. Cost and margin still do not.

findings.title: Somebody logs hours in a colleague's name
findings.expected: It is refused unless they hold the grant for it, because hours are that person's account of their own day.
findings.actual: A consultant logging their own hours is fine; logging Sam's is refused — "Record others' time is not something Functional Consultant can do here. Time is recorded by the person who did the work." A project manager holds the grant and may, and the entry keeps Sam's name while the trail records who typed it.
findings.impact: Hours cannot be attributed to somebody who did not agree they worked them, except by a role the firm chose to trust with it.

findings.title: Actual effort overruns the estimate
findings.expected: The variance is visible on the issue, and it is honest about what it is measured against.
findings.actual: 12h spent against 8h agreed — +4h, 50%. An unestimated issue reports its variance as unknown rather than as an overrun against zero, and an overrun against a draft is labelled as such: a number nobody agreed is not a commitment anybody broke.
findings.stops: before it reaches the project — the variance is per issue, and nothing rolls it up to a milestone, a SOW or a margin
findings.impact: A consultant can see the overrun on the record. A partner still cannot see it on the engagement.

findings.title: A client asks for something outside the SOW
findings.expected: The system can tell that it is outside — and if it cannot judge that, it can at least show what the request costs against what was agreed.
findings.actual: 18h of 40h used (45%), and the current plan needs 54h — 14h more than was agreed. The overrun is arithmetic rather than opinion: agreed effort is on the SOW, planned comes from the estimates, spent comes from the recorded hours. A project attributed to nothing is counted as such (1 here), a draft SOW refuses work ("SOW-2026-015 is draft. Work cannot be delivered under it yet."), and a reference the database would reject is refused here first: "SOW-2026-014 is already recorded against this engagement."
findings.stops: at the judgement — nothing reads the scope statement and decides whether a particular request is inside it
findings.impact: Scope leakage is now measurable where it shows up as effort. Whether a request is in scope remains a commercial call, and the product makes its consequence visible rather than pretending to make the call.

findings.title: A change request is raised
findings.expected: It is captured as a CR, valued, and linked to the work it changes.
findings.actual: A CR can be raised as a work item of type "Change Request" — the type is configuration and had to be added first, linked to the issue that prompted it, and it cannot start until somebody with the authority approves it (scenario P). What it still carries is no value of its own: approving it does not move the agreed effort or value on the statement of work, so a firm sees the overrun rather than the amendment.
findings.stops: at the join — a change request is now a priced record with an approval and an effective date (CR1), and this issue-shaped one is not linked to it. `ChangeRequest.issueId` exists and nothing sets it, so the register and the contract still describe the same change twice.
findings.impact: The valuation gap this described is closed: an approved change moves the contracted position without touching the baseline. What is left is that the issue somebody raises and the variation somebody prices are two records, and only a person knows they are the same change.

findings.title: A change request is approved
findings.expected: The approval is given by somebody with the authority for it, and the work cannot start without it.
findings.actual: Unapproved, the CR cannot start: "Change request approval is needed before this can move to “In Progress”." The consultant who asked cannot answer — "Decide an approval is not something Functional Consultant can do here." — and neither can an analyst, because the rule names the sponsor: "Decide an approval is not something Support Analyst can do here." Once the sponsor approves, the work starts. A rejection blocks the same move and stays on the record: "Change request approval: this was rejected by Dana. Not within this phase — raise it for the next release."
findings.stops: at this issue-shaped change only. Approving a `ChangeRequest` DOES move the contracted position now — baseline plus approved movements, computed on read (CR1) — and the two paths are not yet joined: this scenario approves a work item, not a variation.
findings.impact: A change can no longer be delivered without somebody with authority agreeing to it. What it is worth is still not recorded anywhere.

findings.title: A firm writes an approval rule that nobody can satisfy
findings.expected: The rule is refused, rather than becoming a wall the work never gets past.
findings.actual: A rule with no decider is refused — "“Impossible” names no role that can decide it, so nothing it gates could ever proceed." — and so is one that asks nothing: "“Unasked” asks no question. Somebody has to be told what they are approving." Both would produce work that reaches a status never, and whoever wrote the rule would hear about it weeks later from somebody who could not proceed.
findings.impact: A control that cannot be satisfied is a wall, and the configuration screen refuses to build one.

findings.title: An issue is closed with no evidence attached
findings.expected: Closure is refused, because the resolution could not be produced later.
findings.actual: Refused without evidence: "“Closed - confirmed” needs at least one piece of evidence on the record — that is what makes the closure producible later." Accepted once a sign-off document is attached. Closing as "no defect" needs no evidence but does need a reason, because it makes a claim about the work rather than about the client.
findings.impact: A confirmed closure now has something behind it that can be shown to a client who disputes it.

findings.title: Work is closed as “no defect” with no explanation
findings.expected: The change is refused until somebody says why, and the why survives on the trail.
findings.actual: Refused without a reason: "“Closed - no defect” needs a reason. This is the outcome people ask about months later." With one, the change lands and the trail carries it — "Behaviour is as designed; raised against an out-of-date specification.". The reason is stamped only on the status entry, so a closure rationale is never attributed to an unrelated field in the same save.
findings.impact: The two closures a client queries later now come with the firm’s own explanation attached.

findings.title: An issue is resolved
findings.expected: The resolution is recorded, the client is told, and verification is requested.
findings.actual: The status moves, the next action is recorded and 2 audit entries were written with before, after and actor. No message is sent to the client.
findings.stops: at telling the client
findings.impact: Verification waits on somebody remembering to ask for it.

findings.title: An issue is verified and closed
findings.expected: Closure is recorded with a date, and it cannot be reopened without a trace.
findings.actual: Reached along the route the graph requires — In Progress, Awaiting client confirmation, evidence attached, then closed. Closing derived actualEnd = 2026-08-15; reopening cleared it, and both derived writes are in the trail (2 entries). The derivation guards on the status having changed, so an unrelated edit cannot overwrite a closure date.
findings.impact: Closure and reopening are both honest about the date.

findings.title: An issue jumps straight from Open to Closed, skipping every intermediate state
findings.expected: The transition is refused, and the refusal says where the work can actually go from here.
findings.actual: Refused: "“Open” cannot move straight to “Closed - confirmed”. From here the work can go to: In Progress, Needs clarification, Closed - no defect, Superseded." The same move succeeds along the route the graph allows — In Progress, Awaiting client confirmation, then Closed - confirmed with evidence attached. A patch carrying a refused status is rejected whole, so the other fields in it are not quietly saved.
findings.impact: Closure now requires the steps that make it defensible, and the graph is configuration a firm can change.

findings.title: A firm turns transition enforcement off
findings.expected: Every move is allowed again, and the change is recorded as the decision it is.
findings.actual: With enforcement off the direct close is accepted again, and the switch is audited with before and after. A table that would trap work is refused rather than saved: "Work in “In Progress” could never be closed — no route from it reaches a closing status."
findings.impact: The control is the firm’s to relax, and relaxing it is a recorded decision rather than a silent default.

findings.title: A consultant, an analyst and a client user each try the same nine operations
findings.expected: Each is allowed what their role grants and refused the rest, with a refusal that explains itself.
findings.actual: Consultant may raise, edit, close, reopen, schedule and estimate but not archive or configure. Analyst may raise, edit and note but not close, reopen, schedule or estimate — reopening counts as a closure decision, because it moves a record back out of the done set. Client user may raise and note only. The refusal names the role rather than just saying no: "Close work is not something Client User can do here."
findings.impact: The rules a firm states about who may do what are now applied, and applied at the reducer rather than in the screens.

findings.title: Somebody claims to be a colleague
findings.expected: The claim is checked against an identity provider before anything is allowed.
findings.actual: Entra ID sign-in is built: authorisation-code flow with PKCE, the id token verified against the published keys for issuer, audience and expiry, and the nonce checked against the one this server generated. The session cookie is signed and driven here rather than read — a valid one round-trips, a tampered one and one signed with another key are both refused, and an expired one reports "expired" rather than being quietly accepted. With a provider configured the write endpoint refuses an unverified request; with none configured the application runs as the single operator exactly as before, because a deployment without credentials should work rather than show a login it cannot satisfy.
findings.stops: at the harness, not at the tenant. There IS a real registration now and real people sign in against it — and running it found what constructing it could not: the callback redirected to the internal container address, so a completed sign-in ended on a browser error page. Verified-by-construction is precisely what missed that. AU3 now covers the redirect; the provider handshake itself still cannot be driven here, because that needs a test tenant.
findings.impact: The four environment values are set and grants rest on a proven identity. What remains is that no check in this suite exercises the round trip through a real provider, which is the one class of auth fault that has actually reached production.

findings.title: A deployment starts before its secrets have been written
findings.expected: Nothing is signed or accepted with a value that only looks like a secret.
findings.actual: The unresolved reference is 77 characters, so a length check alone accepts it — and it is refused instead: "AXIOMATE_SESSION_SECRET still holds an unresolved reference rather than a value. The vault…" A placeholder is refused too, a real key is accepted, and the same guard reads both bearer tokens, where an unresolved reference would otherwise have become the accepted token rather than merely a weak signing key.
findings.impact: The deployment that has not had its secrets written yet now refuses to sign or accept anything, rather than working with a value published in its own templates.

findings.title: Somebody edits another person's note
findings.expected: The edit is refused, because a note is that person's account — unless they hold the supervisor grant.
findings.actual: Refused for a different author: "Written by Validator. A note is that person's account of what they saw, so it is theirs to correct." With the supervisor grant it lands, and the note still says it was written by Validator while recording Someone Else as the editor. The rule had existed in the panel since notes shipped and was never checked in the reducer — so it held for people using the button and for nothing else that could dispatch.
findings.impact: Somebody else's account of what they saw can no longer be rewritten under their name — provided they hold a role of their own. An actor with none still falls back to Administrator, which is ST2b.

findings.title: Two people edit the same issue at once
findings.expected: The second write is refused as stale rather than silently overwriting the first.
findings.actual: The second write is refused and names both values: "OAPIL-1 has changed since you opened it: owner is now “Dev”, not “Priya”. Your change was not saved. Reload to see theirs, then decide." The record still reads Dev, so nothing was overwritten. Changing a different field on the same record is allowed — comparing only the fields being written is what stops a due date conflicting with an owner, which is the false conflict that makes people switch optimistic locking off. Once the loser has read the new value their write goes through.
findings.impact: Two consultants working one record are stopped when they genuinely disagree and left alone when they do not, and neither loses work without being told.

findings.title: A record is archived and later restored
findings.expected: Nothing is orphaned, and anything moved out during the archive comes back.
findings.actual: Restoring a child under an archived parent is refused ("“Inventory” is archived, so this would be restored somewhere nothing can see it. Restore that first."), and restoring the parent brings all 3 records back. Deletion is soft throughout; nothing is destroyed.
findings.impact: The data lifecycle is reversible and cannot produce an unreachable record.

findings.title: The firm shortens its High-severity SLA from 5 days to 2
findings.expected: The next issue raised gets a 2-day target, and everything downstream follows.
findings.actual: Default High = 5d proposed 2026-08-10; after the change the same issue proposes 2026-08-05. The policy is read from the model at every derivation, not captured at startup, and the change is audited with before and after.
findings.impact: Configuration reaches runtime for the SLA. Dates already committed are deliberately left alone, and the screen says so.

findings.title: The firm adds a work type and retires another
findings.expected: New records can use the new type, and records already filed under the retired one stay readable.
findings.actual: A new type is usable immediately (true), and retiring one in use is refused: "3 records are classified as "Defect". Reclassify them first.".
findings.impact: The discriminator behaves as configuration, which is what keeps one work-item table honest.

findings.title: A project is created from a template
findings.expected: Work items, workflow, SLA, notifications, agents and checklists all arrive with it.
findings.actual: Adopting "Axiocloud standard delivery" at a scope works and carries 6 agents, 2 workflows, an approval default. It creates no work items, applies no SLA of its own and configures no notifications — a template is a set of defaults, not a project setup.
findings.stops: at everything the template does not carry
findings.impact: Mobilising a project is still manual; only the operating-model defaults are inherited.

findings.title: The daily IMS report is checked against the records it counts
findings.expected: Every figure on the report can be reproduced from the underlying rows.
findings.actual: Report says open=2 and overdue=1; recounting the rows gives 2 and 1. Section "Overdue" lists 1. The report derives from the same rows the grid shows, counts rather than estimates, and prints its own section cap rather than truncating silently.
findings.impact: The one report that exists reconciles to its source.

findings.title: Weekly client and monthly governance reporting
findings.expected: A client-safe weekly pack and a monthly governance pack can be produced.
findings.actual: Only the daily IMS is built (3 report module(s) in source). The weekly pack needs a client-visible boundary that does not exist — no field marks a record or a note as client-safe.
findings.stops: at the visibility boundary
findings.impact: Anything sent to a client is assembled by hand, and internal notes are one copy-paste from the client.

findings.title: Every meaningful change answers who, what, when, before, after and why
findings.expected: The trail is complete enough to defend a decision months later.
findings.actual: 2 entries, all carrying actor, time, field, before and after; 1 carry a reason. Attribution is a parameter of the reducer, so no action can forge it — proven separately by audit:attribution. Why is captured where the product asks for it (date changes, estimate revisions) and absent elsewhere.
findings.stops: at "why" for ordinary field edits
findings.impact: The trail is strong on what changed, thinner on the reasoning behind routine edits.

findings.title: The assistant proposes a change with low confidence
findings.expected: It recommends rather than acts, and a person decides.
findings.actual: One live agent exists behind a chat route, and its proposals are rendered as cards a person accepts or rejects (16 files participate). Confidence thresholds and autonomy levels are registry fields with no runtime that reads them. Driving it needs a model key this script does not have.
findings.stops: at the autonomy fields — declared, unread
findings.impact: 37 of 38 agents are records. The one that runs is gated correctly, but the gate is code, not the configured policy.

findings.title: The database is unreachable while someone is working
findings.expected: The user keeps working, nothing is lost, and the queue recovers when it comes back.
findings.actual: An outage is retried 4 times inline and then the queue pauses rather than ending the session — holding its work and saying "Not saved yet · 3 changes". It starts again the moment connectivity returns, when the tab is looked at again, or after 30s on its own, escalating to 240s and never while the machine reports itself offline. The failures that cannot improve stay stopped through every trigger: a refused change, a malformed request, an oversized batch, a gateway 403, a renamed route, a database constraint the server marked deterministic, and a deployment with no database — the last clearing its queue because there is nothing to deliver to, the others keeping theirs so the unload beacon can still try. What is proven is the policy: `verdictFor` and `shouldResume` are pure and driven directly. A queue actually resuming has never run in a browser, because without a database the endpoint answers `disabled` and stops before the paused path is reachable at all.
findings.stops: at a resume observed in a browser
findings.impact: A ten-second outage no longer ends persistence for the rest of the session. The rule is proven; the recovery it describes has not been watched happen.

findings.title: A malformed or hostile write reaches the API
findings.expected: It is rejected before it touches stored state.
findings.actual: 9 malformed or hostile actions are refused before the database is considered, and 4 legitimate ones — including an empty patch, a concurrency expectation and an idempotency key — still pass. The refusal names the field rather than the request: "Field 'patch' on updateIssue carries unrecognised field 'ownerr'.". The patch is checked field by field, which is the part that matters: the reducer merges an edit with a spread, so an unrecognised key lands in the record and a mistyped one replaces a real field. Whether a status is one this firm uses is left to the reducer, which owns the transition graph and answers with the routes that exist — two lists here would be free to disagree.
findings.impact: A client bug or a hostile caller can no longer write a field the record does not have, or a type it cannot hold.

findings.title: The persistence layer is exercised at all
findings.expected: Writes reach Postgres and reload correctly.
findings.actual: 62 of 62 persistence checks passed against postgresql://***@axiomate-tms-db.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/axiomate_tms, recorded 2026-08-25. The run writes values chosen to break careless mapping and reads the whole workspace back through the ordinary load path: quarter hours as a decimal rather than a float, a zero that must not return as null, money with pennies, a date written as a day, a note keeping its quotes and its newline, an audit reason keeping its punctuation. It also covers the two things only a database can show — that a capped trail keeps the newest entries rather than the oldest, and that the id counter is stored so a restart cannot re-mint an id.
findings.impact: Twenty-one tables, fourteen mapper pairs and a write path with an arm per action have now executed against Postgres rather than only typechecked.

findings.title: A consultant submits a timesheet
findings.expected: The week is presented for approval, and approval freezes exactly what was approved.
findings.actual: A week is the Monday containing a date — 19 August resolves to 2026-08-17. The total is computed from live entries rather than copied onto the sheet: 15.5h, of which 13.5h billable, correctly excluding the next week, another person, and a withdrawn entry. Submitting an open week succeeds; submitting it twice is refused with "The week of 17 Aug is already submitted and awaiting approva"; submitting somebody else's week is refused even holding the permission, because a timesheet is a personal attestation. A week that is not a Monday is refused rather than rounded. An EMPTY week submits — "I was on leave" is a claim, and refusing it strands the one person with nothing to report. Once submitted the week is frozen and the freeze reports which state it is in (Submitted here, Approved once approved) rather than a boolean, because "awaiting approval" and "already approved" call for different next moves. The next week and another person stay open.
findings.stops: nowhere in the rules. submitTimesheet calls these, U2 drives the freeze through the reducer, and the persistence proof shows a submitted week surviving a reload. What no check here opens is the screen — the Submit control is verified by construction, as the row menu is.
findings.impact: Hours can now be signed off, which is what makes them billable. The rules are driven here directly, so a mistake in them is found before any caller is involved.

findings.title: A submitted timesheet is rejected
findings.expected: The rejection returns specific entries, says why, and the corrected resubmission is traceable.
findings.actual: The person who submitted cannot decide their own week — refused with "A timesheet is decided by somebody other than the person who submitted" — and that holds even though this actor DOES hold the approve permission, because a self-approval is not a weaker control but the absence of one. Approving needs no reason; returning needs one, refused otherwise with "Returning a timesheet needs a reason — the person has to kno": "yes" is complete on its own, "no" leaves somebody guessing what to change. A returned week is editable again — isFrozen answers null — and resubmits cleanly, which is the whole correction loop. Deciding a week twice is refused and names which way it already went. The reason travels on the row, so what was returned and why is answerable later without reconstructing it.
findings.stops: nowhere in the rules. decideTimesheet calls these, and the persistence proof shows a returned week keeping its reason and becoming editable again after a reload — both halves of the loop, not just the refusal.
findings.impact: The correction loop exists for the record that drives revenue, and the rule that stops a self-approval is driven rather than asserted — through the reducer as well as here.

findings.title: A submitted week refuses edits, and every other week does not
findings.expected: Hours inside a submitted week cannot be added, changed or withdrawn — and nothing else is affected.
findings.actual: Once the week of 03 Aug is submitted, all three time arms refuse inside it: "The week of 03 Aug is submitted and awaiting approval. Hours cannot be cha". Moving an entry OUT of the week is refused too — the check reads the stored date and, when a patch moves it, the destination as well, so an hour cannot walk out of a week somebody has attested to by editing the one field the freeze exists to hold. Everything else stays open: the next week, another person, and the same entry once the week is returned. Approved freezes again and says so differently ("The week of 03 Aug is approved. Hours cannot be chan"), because "awaiting approval" and "already approved" call for different next moves. A rejection carries its reason on the row, and the person who submitted cannot approve their own week even holding the grant.
findings.stops: nowhere in the rules, and nowhere in storage either — the Timesheet table landed in the commit after this scenario was written, and the persistence proof drives a submitted week through Postgres and finds the freeze still holding. What no check here opens is the screen.
findings.impact: The freeze is the point of the feature: without it an approver signs off a number that can change underneath them. Both directions are asserted, because a guard that only refuses is indistinguishable from a broken feature.

findings.title: A notification fails to deliver
findings.expected: The failure is visible and recorded — a silent non-delivery is the dangerous case.
findings.actual: The message is recorded with an outcome rather than attempted and lost: delivery is "pending" because "Queued for the scheduled pass to email." The scheduled pass drains this queue through the same Graph client as client mail and stamps what actually happened; the raise itself stays honest about not having sent anything yet. The undelivered count is shown to everybody rather than hidden behind a setting.
findings.stops: at the live send — the drain runs in production through Graph, which this harness cannot drive; Teams still has nowhere to go
findings.impact: Non-delivery is visible, counted, and — for email — drained by the next pass.

findings.title: The assistant recommends something wrong
findings.expected: A person rejects it, the rejection is recorded, and the original recommendation is preserved.
findings.actual: Proposals are rendered as cards a person accepts or rejects (3 chat module(s) implement it), and an accepted proposal goes through the same reducer as a human edit, so it is audited identically. A rejection changes nothing and is recorded nowhere — no rejection log exists in source — so the system cannot learn which recommendations were wrong.
findings.stops: at the rejection — it disappears
findings.impact: Agent quality cannot be measured, because only the accepted half of its output is kept.

findings.title: An automation fails part-way through
findings.expected: The run stops safely, what did happen is visible, and the failure is recorded rather than swallowed.
findings.actual: The working step ran and the impossible one did not: 1 notification raised, 1 step refused ("That approval rule no longer exists."), and the original change stands. A rule addressed to a role nobody holds reports it — "Reached nobody — "role:ROLE_CLIENT_SPONSOR" resolves to no one in the directory." — rather than looking like it worked. Rules act by dispatching ordinary actions, so a rule cannot do anything a person could not, and everything it does is in the trail with the rule that caused it.
findings.stops: at the schedule — every rule reacts to something that happened, so "every morning, escalate what is about to breach" cannot be expressed
findings.impact: Event-driven automation works and fails safely. Time-driven automation needs a clock and a process to run it, and this application has neither.

findings.title: An integration fails
findings.expected: The failure is contained, retried where safe, surfaced, and never leaves records half-written.
findings.actual: No outbound integration exists. The only network call the product makes is to the model behind the chat route; an integration client exists.
findings.stops: at the integration
findings.impact: Nothing to fail yet — but the write path has no idempotency key, so retries will need one before the first integration lands. See FL4.

findings.title: The same write is delivered twice
findings.expected: The second delivery is recognised and ignored, rather than creating a second record.
findings.actual: Three writes are delivered, then re-delivered with a fourth appended — the overlap a closing tab produces. The second delivery applies 1 and recognises 3 as already done, leaving 4 notes. Without the key the same delivery leaves 7. A key repeated inside one batch collapses to one, an unkeyed action always applies — intake and the scheduled pass write without one — and a malformed key is refused at the route rather than dropped, so protection can never be silently off. Against Postgres on 2026-08-25: the same batch delivered twice left the second delivery writing nothing, the keys are stored so the skip survives a restart, and a refused keyed batch named exactly the key that committed.
findings.impact: Hiding a tab mid-save no longer duplicates notes, evidence and dependencies. The rule is proven; the storage behind it is still unexercised, like every other database claim in this repository.

findings.title: A working pattern changes, and last quarter still has to add up
findings.expected: What was true is preserved with its period, and a later correction cannot move a figure already computed.
findings.actual: A date before any period returns null rather than a default, and so does a person nobody has a pattern for — which is the property the rest rests on, because a fallback would still return a plausible number. `validTo` is exclusive: 30 June answers 7.5h and 1 July answers 6h, so two periods can abut without overlapping. An overlap is refused — "That period overlaps one already recorded: 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-01. T…" — while a gap is allowed, because somebody who left and rejoined has one and forcing contiguity would invent employment. Correcting a period against itself is permitted. A correction reports the 1 record computed from that version and moves none of it: the stamp still holds 7.5h from ver-1. What is not proven is the round trip — no version has been stored, and nothing in the application stamps anything yet, because the first thing that will is an approved timesheet.
findings.stops: at storage, and at a stamp made by the application rather than by this scenario
findings.impact: The rules hold. Until they are wired to capacity and persisted, a working pattern is still a single value that a change destroys.

findings.title: A consultant records time against work that has run past its due date
findings.expected: The overrun warns and never refuses; only a closed issue shuts the window, and a derived opening date says it was derived.
findings.actual: Three days past the due date and still open, the entry is allowed and carries a warning — "Logged 3 days after the due date (2026-08-10). Still open." — rather than a refusal, because a control that fires on every overrunning issue stops being a control. The window shuts when the issue does: a closed record refuses and names the route, "Hours genuinely spent on closed work can still be recorded, with a reason and an approval to reopen the window — that is what the extension is for.". The opening date is 2026-08-03 with provenance `default` and the words "opens at the raised date — no start date set", so a window derived from the raised date can never be read as a plan somebody set; a recorded start date reports `stated` instead. A day before the window is refused, the opening day itself is not. Somebody else's hours refuse without `time.recordForOthers` and are allowed with it — the design writes that permission `time.logForOthers`, which does not exist, so the real key is used. A submitted week is frozen and a returned one is editable again. **And `addTime` now consults all of it**: an entry on the opening day is accepted, one the day before is refused ("2026-08-01 is before OAPIL-1's time entry window, which open…"), and one against a closed issue is refused with the route out (" to reopen the window — that is what the extension is for."). The authority rule stays where it was, deliberately — this module asks whether the person owns the ISSUE, and the reducer asks whether the actor may record for the PERSON, which would have started refusing a consultant logging their own hours on a colleague's work.
findings.stops: at the screen. The refusals are enforced and the extension route they name — logging against a closed issue with a reason and an approval — has no UI, so today the answer is to reopen the issue. `updateTime` also does not consult the window: an entry can still be edited onto a date the window would have refused.
findings.impact: Time could be logged against closed work and against dates before the work existed. Both are now refused, and an overrunning issue still warns rather than refusing — which is what keeps the refusal meaningful.

findings.title: A daily cap is checked against a working pattern nobody recorded
findings.expected: The cap is reported unenforced rather than defaulted to eight, and a late entry has to explain itself only past the allowance.
findings.actual: A date before any pattern, a person nobody has a pattern for, and a version whose value carries no hours per day all answer unenforced with a null cap — three ways of not knowing, none of them eight. An unenforced cap warns about nothing, so an eleven-hour day is recorded rather than argued with. Where a pattern exists the cap is read at the work date, not at today: 30 June is 7.5h from ver-7 and 1 July is 6h from ver-8, so hours logged in June are checked against June even after a move to a four-day week. Eleven hours against a 7.5h day warns and does not refuse — long days happen, and refusing one produces hours booked to the wrong day rather than fewer hours worked. Backdating turns at exactly 7 days: 7 days late needs nothing, 8 days late needs a justification and an approval. No cap is applied by anything, and no working pattern has been recorded as a version by the application.
findings.stops: at the name join. `addTime` now reports a long day as a warning beside the confirmation, but `Version` keys on a directory id while `TimeEntry.person` holds a name — so a person whose name does not resolve gets no cap and therefore no warning. It fails to a missing remark rather than a wrong refusal, which is why it was acceptable to wire at all.
findings.impact: The honest answer is available. Until patterns are versioned and the cap is called, a daily total is unchecked — which is better than checked against a number nobody entered.

findings.title: A person signs in and is sent back to an address that exists
findings.expected: Sign-in and sign-out return the browser to the public address somebody typed, not to whatever this process answers on.
findings.actual: A request delivered to the container at https://cd04369db00c:8080 with the proxy's own headers resolves to https://axiomate-tms.azurewebsites.net, which is where the browser came from. Two proxies deep it still takes the client's view (https://axiomate-tms.azurewebsites.net) rather than the gateway's. With no forwarded headers it falls back to the configured Entra redirect URI (https://axiomate-tms.azurewebsites.net) — trustworthy because Entra refuses an unregistered redirect, so a deployment that gets this wrong cannot sign anybody in. With neither, on a developer's machine, the request's own origin is correct and is used (http://localhost:3000). The Secure flag on the session cookie is decided from the same origin, so it is now a fact about the address the browser used rather than about an internal one.
findings.stops: nowhere — but only the origin is proven here; that the deployed site sends the forwarded header is a property of App Service, verified by reading a Location header from the running site
findings.impact: Sign-in and sign-out both ended on a browser error page for every user, and every check inside the process passed. A redirect is only correct relative to something outside the process, which is why this asserts against a proxied request rather than a plain one.

findings.title: Capacity is computed against the working week in force at the time
findings.expected: A period is checked against the pattern recorded for it, and a figure resting on an assumption says so.
findings.actual: A date before anything was recorded resolves to the stored profile, which reports itself as a default — NOT to a version that does not exist, and not to a fabricated eight. Where a pattern is in force it wins and is marked stated, read at the work date rather than at today: April is 8h over 5 days, July is 6h over 4, so an allocation running in April is checked against April even after a move to a four-day week. A version whose value carries no usable hours resolves to the stored profile rather than a zero-hour day. Somebody with neither a profile nor a version resolves to nothing at all. The null does not propagate into capacityFor — it must answer, because it is what refuses an overallocation — so the PROVENANCE does instead: position.basis is stated against a recorded pattern and default against an assumed one, and describeCapacity says so out loud in the second case and not the first.
findings.stops: nowhere for the working pattern. A pattern that changes mid-allocation is read at the START of the window rather than splitting it — that is a different feature, and it would change what capacityFor returns rather than how it is called
findings.impact: A capacity figure computed from an assumed working week is not wrong, but it is a different claim from one computed from a confirmed week — and the difference now travels with the number instead of being lost the moment it is quoted.

findings.title: A cost is computed from the rate in force on the day the work was done
findings.expected: Hours are priced at their own date, an unrated hour makes the total absent rather than smaller, and nobody without the grant is sent a rate at all.
findings.actual: A date before any rate answers null and does NOT fall back — there is no defensible shipped rate for a person, so unlike a working pattern this one cannot default and label the default. Where a rate is in force it is read at the WORK date: 2 March costs 40 and 3 August costs 50, so a pay rise in July does not retrospectively change what March cost. Cost and bill are separate rows and move independently. Twenty hours across the two periods come to 900 cost against 2000 billed — margin 1100 at 55%. Add four hours from before any rate and the WHOLE total goes absent rather than smaller: 4h of 14h unrated, cost null. A partial sum presented as a total is the failure this refuses — it looks like an answer and is short by an unknown amount. Mixed currencies are absent for the same reason. Overlapping periods are refused by lib/versioning's own check rather than a second implementation of the boundary rule.
findings.stops: at the timesheet — nothing feeds worked hours into this yet, and no screen records a rate. Cost is computable and not yet computed.
findings.impact: This is the number the whole commercial half of the product was missing. It is deliberately absent rather than approximate whenever any hour in the set is unpriced, because a margin that is quietly short is worse than one that is missing.

findings.title: A change is agreed, and what was originally signed is still answerable
findings.expected: An approved change moves the contracted position without touching the baseline, and a pending one is reported separately rather than added in.
findings.actual: Signed at 400h and GBP 1,00,000, and BOTH are still exactly that after two approved changes — the movements live on the changes, never on the statement of work, so "what did we originally agree" stays answerable however many variations follow. The approved movements net to 60h and 15,000, a descoping counting as the negative it is, giving 460h and 1,15,000 contracted today. A submitted change worth 60,000 is reported alongside and is NOT in that figure — a client-facing total quietly including a request nobody agreed to is the most damaging thing this could do. Refused, draft and withdrawn contribute nothing. As at a date the effective date governs, not the decision date: June sees 1000 and September sees 2000 from the same two approved changes. The person who raised it cannot decide it even holding the grant, refusing needs a reason, and a change moving neither effort nor value is refused as a clarification rather than inflating the count of variations a client is told they asked for.
findings.stops: at the screen and at the SOW panel — nothing raises or decides a change request from the UI yet, and sowPosition still reads the baseline rather than the contracted position
findings.impact: Scope change is the commonest commercial event in consulting and it had nowhere to live: a work-type string on an issue, and a SOW status that said a variation happened without saying what it was worth.

findings.title: A piece of work needs somebody who can do it, and the shortlist says what it cannot see
findings.expected: Recorded skill produces candidates rather than a recommendation, a stale skill is marked rather than dropped, and a level nobody may read shortens the list visibly rather than silently.
findings.actual: Asked for Intercompany at practitioner and X++ at working: 1 person meets both (AMOLAK) and 2 meet part of it (DHARMENDRA, MICHAEL). Jaya holds Intercompany at Aware, below the floor, so she is not on the list; Priya's row is withdrawn and Tarun's skill has been retired from the catalogue, so neither produces a candidate. Dharmendra last used it in 2021 and nobody has said when Michael last used his — both are marked stale rather than dropped, because a firm may have nobody fresher and hiding them would answer a different question. Nothing is ranked and no best match is returned: the result carries the four things it cannot see — who the client already knows and trusts; who was on the call last week — and describeMatch says so in the sentence. Read by somebody without skill.view, the same data yields 0 candidates and reports 5 unreadable rows, so a shortlist shortened by a permission announces itself instead of looking like an empty firm; Amolak reading it still finds himself, because a person's own rows are never withheld from them.
findings.stops: at demand. Nothing yet asks a deliverable what skills it needs, so the requirements above are constructed here rather than read off a work item — this answers "who could do this" only once somebody states what "this" needs. It is also deliberately not joined to availability or cost: both now exist, and combining them into one ranked answer is the delivery decision lib/capacity.ts refuses to make.
findings.impact: Capacity could say whether a plan was possible and never who should be on it. This closes one of the three gaps capacity.ts names — skill — and leaves the other two, client relationship and who was on the call last week, absent and stated as absent rather than quietly assumed away.

findings.title: A consultant records their own skills, and cannot rewrite what somebody else said about them
findings.expected: Self-rated is yours to record, correct and retract. An assessed level is the assessor’s, and the two arms agree about that rather than one being stricter than the other.
findings.actual: A consultant holding skill.record may record her own skills self-rated, and that is the case the grant exists for — a directory only a lead may write to stays empty. She may not certify herself ("Assess somebody's skill is not something Functional Consultant can do here. You can record your own skills as self-rated; saying they are assessed or certified is somebody else's judgement to record."), which is what stops the product showing a certification nobody issued, and she may not record against a colleague ("Assess somebody's skill is not something Functional Consultant can do here. Recording a level against another person needs the grant for it."). A second row for the same person and skill is refused, because "what level is she at" must not have two answers. Somebody holding skill.assess then records an assessed level about her. She can neither correct it ("Assess somebody's skill is not something Functional Consultant can do here. You can correct your own self-rated level; assessed and certified are not yours to set.") nor withdraw it ("Assess somebody's skill is not something Functional Consultant can do here. This level was assessed by somebody else, so withdrawing it is theirs to do. Ask Nishant Sekhar if it is wrong.") — and those two agreeing is the point: the first version let her delete a signed judgement she was not allowed to correct, so the stronger act had the weaker gate. Her own self-rated row stays hers to correct and to retract.
findings.impact: A level is a claim with somebody’s name on it. This is what keeps the name attached to the person who made the claim, in both directions — nobody can award themselves a credential, and nobody can quietly delete one written about them.

findings.title: A file is attached to an issue, and a record only ever exists when the bytes do
findings.expected: Uploads are refused on size, on an executable, and on a path in the name; the same file cannot be attached twice to one record; and a store nobody has configured refuses loudly rather than accepting and dropping.
findings.actual: Refused before anything is stored: a file over the 25.0 MB limit, an empty one, "setup.exe" ("“.exe” files are not accepted — their purpose is to execute. Put it in a zip if it genuinely needs to travel with the record."), and a name carrying a path. "OAPIL_backup.axmodel" is accepted — a deny list rather than an allow list, because an allow list would refuse real consulting work weekly until somebody widened it into uselessness. The reducer refuses a document against an issue that does not exist ("That record no longer exists, so there is nothing to attach the file to.") and against a kind of thing documents cannot hang off, which is what stops an orphan holding real bytes that nothing lists. The same checksum on the same issue is refused as a double-click; on a different issue it is allowed, because one specification genuinely does attach to two records. A consultant cannot withdraw somebody else's attachment ("Withdraw somebody else's file is not something Functional Consultant can do here. Validator attached this."); the person who attached it always can, and withdrawing is soft and leaves the file in the library rather than reaching through to delete it. A store nobody has configured refuses every call with its reason instead of accepting and dropping, which is the failure a stub would produce by being helpful.
findings.stops: at a consented document library — see D. Every rule above is exercised; no byte has yet been through Graph.
findings.impact: The record and the artefact are now the same fact. What is still missing is one administrator action, not a feature.

findings.title: A milestone is delivered, accepted, and worth what it was worth on the day it was signed
findings.expected: Delivery and acceptance are separate answers, an approved change moves a pending milestone and never an accepted one, and a schedule that does not add up says so instead of being refused.
findings.actual: A 25/35/25/15 schedule on a £100k contract. Milestone 1 was accepted before a £20k change was approved, and it is still worth £25,000 — the figure was fixed at acceptance, because moving it would retroactively change what the client already signed off. Milestone 3 has not been accepted, so it follows the contracted position and is now worth £30,000 rather than £25,000. 2 milestones are delivered and 1 is delivered and awaiting acceptance — the pair the audit records as unanswerable. £25,000 is billable, which is the accepted one only: delivery does not make money owed unless the contract says it does, and the firm's own "50% upfront" shape proves the reverse case, where signature does. Milestone 1 was accepted with no signed certificate on file, which is allowed and counted rather than blocked — the document library is one consent short, and a milestone that could not be accepted without an artefact would be unusable until that landed. A retainer with no milestones reports "No milestones are recorded against this statement of work. T…" rather than 0% billed. A half-entered schedule reports what is unallocated instead of being refused, because a firm typing four milestones passes through 25, 60 and 85 on the way to 100.
findings.stops: at the invoice. A milestone can now say it is billable and nothing raises an invoice from it — `Invoice` and `InvoiceLine` are the next entity, and the audit sequences them after rates, which now exist.
findings.impact: The commercial spine can answer what is owed and why. It could previously answer only what was contracted in total.

findings.title: A version recorded against the wrong person can be withdrawn — and only then
findings.expected: Removing a version is refused while its subject is still in the directory, so the one gap in effective dating is closed without opening a way to erase somebody’s history.
findings.actual: A version whose subject is not in the directory can be withdrawn, and after it is, valueAt answers null for that person on every date. One whose subject IS in the directory is refused — "Priya is still in the directory, so this is part of their history. Correct it rather than removing it." — which is the guard that keeps this from being a way to erase somebody's dated history: a working pattern deleted quietly would change what capacity answered for past weeks with nothing left to say why. A subject kind the rule does not recognise is refused too ("Only a person's versions can be withdrawn this way, and this one is “sow.value”.") rather than waved through, because subjectKind is open by design and a guard that permitted everything unfamiliar would grow into the general delete this is not.
findings.stops: at a UI. There is no screen for this — it exists for cleaning up after a directory record is removed, which is a script-shaped job today. `correctVersion` is in the same position and the audit records both.
findings.impact: Effective dating could record and correct, and never withdraw. A version recorded against the wrong person was permanent, which made the identity cleanup impossible to finish.

findings.title: A client sends HTML mail and a consultant can read it
findings.expected: Markup becomes text, links survive with their targets, and plain text is passed through byte for byte.
findings.actual: An Outlook body becomes something a person can read: the stylesheet is removed with its contents rather than left in the description, `<o:p>` and every other MSO artefact is gone, `&` and `–` decode, and a bulleted list reads as a list. **Links keep their targets** — "Microsoft guidance (https://learn.microsoft.com/dynamics365/)" — which is the specific thing the Content Conversion connector would have discarded and the reason `infra/intake.bicep` rejected it. A link whose text is already its address is not repeated. Plain text comes back byte for byte, so a text/plain message is never rewritten by a function that exists for markup. Nothing is hard-wrapped, which was the connector's other failing. A client quoting code as `&lt;` gets `<` and not `<`: one decoding pass, because a second is corruption rather than tidying.
findings.stops: at the mailbox. The original message is not kept — it stays in the mailbox intake names in its provenance note, and storing a second copy of every client email as markup nobody reads would be a cost with no reader. Attachments are still not captured; the Logic App appends a line saying where they are.
findings.impact: Client mail arrived as raw markup and a consultant had to read tags to find the request. The conversion was always going to be needed somewhere; doing it here rather than in the connector is what keeps the links.

findings.title: A statement of work says what it will deliver, and agreeing it is a separate act
findings.expected: Scope is recorded before it is agreed, only agreed lines count toward the total, and the total is compared with the contract rather than enforced against it.
findings.actual: Six lines of scope: four agreed, two recorded and not yet agreed. Only the agreed work counts toward the total — 740h, with the unagreed 900h reported beside it rather than added in, because a line somebody typed while reading a draft is not scope and its hours must not reach a figure that gets compared with a contract. That comparison is made and never enforced: against a 1,000h contract it says "contract carries more than the scope does.", and against 500h it says the agreed scope is more than was sold. Both are findings for a person, not refusals — a firm entering forty deliverables passes through every intermediate total on the way. An assumption cannot carry hours ("A assumption is a statement about the agreement, not work somebody does, so it carries no hours."). Scope is one level deep: a criterion hangs off the deliverable it judges and reads directly beneath it, and hanging one off another criterion is refused, which is what stops a scope list quietly becoming a work breakdown.
findings.stops: at delivery. This answers whether a line is in the agreed scope; it does not yet answer whether it has been delivered or accepted. Those are the two axes `lib/milestone.ts` already implements, and adding a second copy before deciding how a delivered deliverable relates to an accepted milestone would duplicate the model rather than reuse it — the baseline decision in the operating-model document. `source: extracted` also has no producer: SOW intelligence needs a document library that is one consent short.
findings.impact: What a contract says it will deliver was a paragraph of free text. It is now a list somebody can agree line by line, compare against the contracted effort, and hang acceptance criteria from.

findings.title: A consultant asks what to do next, and gets an answer they can argue with
findings.expected: Work is gathered from six collections and grouped by why it wants somebody — decisions other people are blocked on first — with no priority score anywhere.
findings.actual: One consultant, six collections, one list: 1 awaiting her decision, 2 past its date, 1 blocked, 1 week of her own hours unsubmitted, 0 otherwise open. Decisions sort first and the sentence says why — "The one awaiting your decision is holding somebody else up." — because a decision is the only thing on the list that is stopping another person. Within a group the order is the date, oldest first. The rank is three parts and all three are visible: reason, then **severity**, then age. OAPIL-1 (High) sorts above OAPIL-2 (Medium) even though OAPIL-2 is four days older — an earlier version of this ordered on date alone and called itself "no priority score", which hid that severity was weighted at zero. No blended number is shown or stored; every row instead names what placed it ("Validator raised it. +40h, and not in the contracted total until decided."). A change request she raised herself would not appear, because the reducer would refuse her decision on it and a row that cannot be acted on is worse than no row. And the two empty lists are different answers: somebody with nothing to do is told so, while somebody the directory does not know is told the join failed — "Nothing here is matched to you: “Nobody At All” is not in …" — because a person shown an empty in-tray concludes they are up to date.
findings.stops: at the name join. Work is found by matching a display name against `Issue.owner` and `Timesheet.person`, so somebody whose directory name differs from the name on their issues sees an empty list. That is the structural gap pending-actions records, and it is reported here rather than hidden — `unrecognised` is a distinct answer from empty.
findings.impact: A consultant deciding what to do next had to read a tree organised by client and project, which is the wrong axis for the question. Their work is now in one place, ordered by an argument they can see and disagree with.

findings.title: A partner asks which engagement is in trouble
findings.expected: Every engagement on one screen, each stating what it has overdue, blocked, unowned or gone quiet — as counts that can be checked, with no score anywhere.
findings.actual: 2 engagements on one screen, ordered by what most wants attention. The OAPIL engagement reports "1 past its date, 1 blocked, 1 with no owner" — three claims, each a count that resolves to rows somebody can open, rather than a percentage or a colour. Concerns are ordered by argument, not by size: a date that has passed is a commitment already broken, so it outranks a blocked item being honestly waited on, which outranks work nobody owns. Nesting is handled where it actually bites — "Phase 2" sits under the engagement and gets no line of its own, but its issue is in the engagement's 3, and across every line each of the 3 live issues is counted exactly once. An earlier version listed both tiers and reported every engagement twice with doubled totals.
findings.stops: short of money. Contracted value, milestones accepted and what is unbillable are all derivable and none of them are shown, because there is no read grant for commercial figures — `sow.edit` is a write permission, and gating a read on it would conflate two questions. A commercial column also needs what `rate.view` and `skill.view` get: withholding from the page payload rather than hiding on screen.
findings.impact: A partner running three engagements had no screen that showed more than one at a time, so "which of these needs me" meant opening each and holding the comparison in their head.

findings.title: Somebody asks what this workspace can do, and is told what it cannot
findings.expected: Every capability is listed with whether it is reachable, and a permission no role holds is reported as a gap rather than shown as off.
findings.actual: 22 capabilities, each naming the permissions it cannot work without and the live roles that hold them. Against this workspace every one is reachable. Take “time.approve” away from every role and exactly one row changes: Timesheets reports "unreachable", names the missing permission, and additionally reports that the product grants it by default while these stored roles do not — which is the failure AC1 was written after and could not itself detect. The two states are kept apart deliberately: OFF is a decision somebody made, UNREACHABLE is nobody having decided anything, and a single indicator covering both would hide the second behind the first.
findings.stops: at the catalogue being written by hand. A capability is a thing a person recognises and the code has no such concept — deriving the list from module names would produce a list of files — so something built and never added here is invisible to this screen. The count is asserted so the omission surfaces as a failing scenario rather than as silence.
findings.impact: Five permissions once existed in code with no stored role holding any of them, so nobody could submit a timesheet, approve one, see a rate, set one or decide a change request. Four features, all working, all unusable, and nothing said so. That state is now visible on a screen.

findings.title: A firm sets a target and cannot fudge how it is doing against it
findings.expected: A goal names a measure the register computes, there is no field to enter progress into, and a measure or scope that no longer resolves reports that rather than zero.
findings.actual: A goal names a measure and a part of the tree, and the figure is computed on every read. Two are set here over the same engagement: a ceiling ("3 open against a ceiling of 2, over by 1. 46 days left.") and a target ("0 of 10 issues, 10 short. 46 days left."). They are deliberately not one shape — a ceiling at 40% of its limit is healthy and a target at 40% is behind, so no percentage is shown for either. **There is no field to enter progress into**, and the stored record is checked for one: id, name, scopeId, measure, target, by, from, note, createdBy, createdAt, deletedAt. Six ways of setting a goal that could never be met are refused with six different sentences — no name, an unknown measure ("“vibes” is not a measure. A goal has to name one the register can compute."), a scope that is not a node, a negative target, no date, and a window that starts after the date it is judged on. Every one of those would otherwise render as a goal sitting at zero, which reads as failure rather than as misconfiguration.
findings.stops: at four measures. Only what the register can count is offered — work closed, open held under, unowned held under, and hours held under — and hours roll up through `TimeEntry.issueId` rather than matching a person by name, because that join is the one already known to fail silently. Milestones accepted and scope agreed are derivable and deliberately absent: they are commercial figures with no read grant, and adding them as a goal measure would reintroduce through a goal what was declined in the portfolio.
findings.impact: A firm could state targets in a document and measure them by asking people how they were doing. The measure is now the register itself, and nobody can type a number into it.

findings.title: A permission is added to the product and somebody can actually use it
findings.expected: Every permission the code defines is granted to at least one shipped role, so a new feature is not born unusable.
findings.actual: All 44 permissions the code defines are granted to at least one shipped role. No grant names a key that does not exist, which would grant nothing while reading as a control. The administrator holds every one, which is what keeps the role able to repair a configuration that has locked somebody out. What this cannot see is a LIVE workspace whose stored grants predate a key: mergeModel lets stored win, so a permission added after a firm was seeded reaches nobody until scripts/reconcile-grants.ts is run. That is a database question, not a code one, and it is reported there.
findings.stops: at the stored model — this proves the shipped defaults are complete, not that a running deployment has caught up with them
findings.impact: Four features shipped usable-looking and unusable before this existed. The failure is silent by construction: the key is checked, the screen renders, and the refusal reads like a permissions decision somebody made.

findings.title: An issue changes owner, and eight dependent areas should follow
findings.expected: Work, capacity, notifications, activity history, audit, reporting and AI context all reflect the new owner.
findings.actual: 4 of 8 dependent areas follow the change — the work item, the audit trail, activity history, the daily report. The other four are absent rather than stale: resource workload, capacity, notifications, AI context. Nothing derived is stored, so within the areas that exist there is no drift to find: the report recomputes from the same rows the grid does.
findings.stops: at the four areas that have no entity behind them
findings.impact: Propagation is correct as far as it goes. It goes half as far as the operating model describes.

findings.title: A board drag asks the same transition rules as the grid
findings.expected: Illegal moves are refused in the policy’s own words; a closing status needing a reason asks for one before dispatch; missing evidence refuses with the message naming it
findings.actual: lanes are exactly the configured statuses and every card counted once; Open→Awaiting refused with checkTransition’s message; Closed - no defect asks for a reason; Closed - confirmed without evidence refused naming evidence; Open→In Progress ok

findings.title: The calendar admits to what it cannot show
findings.expected: dated + undated equals every card under the filter, the sentence states the undated count, and no placed span leaks outside its month
findings.actual: 0 dated + 3 undated = 3; sentence carries the undated count; 0 in month; placements stay inside the month; every week has seven days

findings.title: The cadence arithmetic: clamping, catch-up, and the strictly-after guard
findings.expected: Day 31 means last-of-month everywhere; a stale rule owes exactly one occurrence; a same-day re-run owes nothing; a disabled rule owes nothing
findings.actual: Feb clamps to 28 (29 in a leap year); a rule stale since June owes only July 31; the guard is strictly-after so a raised occurrence is never re-raised; a disabled rule owes nothing; the subject carries the occurrence date

findings.title: A recurrence rule is validated where it is written
findings.expected: A scope that cannot hold an issue is refused with the message naming it; a valid rule is stored; lastRaisedOn cannot be invented at configuration time
findings.actual: a company-scoped rule is refused naming the kind; a valid engagement-scoped rule stores with lastRaisedOn null; a nameless rule is refused saying why

findings.title: The pass raises once, advances the guard, and a same-day re-run raises nothing
findings.expected: First run: one issue with the occurrence-stamped subject, Open, machine-attributed, lastRaisedOn advanced to the occurrence. Second run: zero raised. A rule whose scope has since vanished refuses without advancing.
findings.actual: raised OAPIL-004 “Weekly status — 2026-08-15” Open/Unassigned, machine-attributed; lastRaisedOn advanced to the occurrence; same-day re-run raised nothing
