findings.title: A form submission is classified through the same half as mail

findings.title: The round-trip: extract from an engagement, apply to a fresh parent, reproduce the shape
findings.expected: Same tiers and items under the new parent, a dated item re-anchored to the named day, an undated item still undated, and the dependency reproduced between the mapped ids

findings.actual: unticking Inventory kept its 3 children out of the apply; the archived target refused every create with the guard’s own message and created nothing

findings.actual: v1 at creation, v1 after a rename, v2 after an entries edit, still v2 after the applications append; an empty blueprint is refused saying it would build nothing

findings.actual: Assigning Priya stores her directory id on the issue and on the assignment notice; two entries sharing a name resolve to null rather than a guess; after a rename her My Work and inbox still hold the records by id while the abandoned name honestly matches nothing; a pre-migration row with a null id still joins by name; a role-addressed notification keeps toId null.

findings.title: What the client sees was decided per record, and nothing else leaves
findings.expected: Internal creation is born internal; a client’s own submission and an intake arrival are born visible; marking is editing; the withheld view keeps marked content with its ancestors and empties the machinery.
findings.actual: Internal creation is born internal; Carol’s own submission and an intake arrival are born visible; the flag flips through ordinary edits and the one new document arm; the withheld view keeps the marked record with its ancestor chain, the marked note and the flagged document, empties every commercial and people table, filters audit to surviving records, and the grant screen refuses internal.view on a client role.

findings.title: A late entry explains itself, at whatever allowance the firm set
findings.expected: The allowance is policy, not a constant: set to 3, an entry 3 days late records freely, 4 days late is refused without a reason and recorded with one, and a correction to a stale entry is gated the same way — the audit row saying how late.
findings.actual: The allowance is read from the operating model, refused outside 0–60 in the module’s words, and the shipped default stays 7. At an allowance of 3: exactly 3 days late records with no reason asked; 4 days late is refused naming both numbers and records with a reason, which is stored on the entry and stamped on the audit row as “4 days late”. Correcting a stale entry’s hours is gated identically — refused bare, recorded with its reason — while relabelling its billing passes untouched, because it changes no claimed number.

findings.title: The allocation cap holds, at whichever hardness the firm set
findings.expected: Shipped hard, nobody can be committed past capacity — the override flag included; advisory restores the recorded two-step; the judgement underneath never moves.
findings.actual: The cap ships hard and an over-capacity allocation is refused with and without the override flag, the refusal naming the Configuration screen. Advisory, set through the real op, restores the recorded two-step — warned bare, accepted with the flag, the acceptance audited as “Deliberately overallocated” with the numbers. Hard again shuts the door on the same flag, both mode changes sit in the audit trail, an invalid mode is refused by the op, and a single allocation past 100% refuses identically in both modes because the judgement underneath never moved.

findings.title: The person’s own say over each kind, with the default path untouched
findings.expected: No pref means exactly today’s behaviour — the regression guard runs first; email adds a pending record for the drain; mute mints nothing but the audit still answers why; preferences are self-or-admin; role labels have no preferences.
findings.actual: With no preference set an assignment mints exactly one delivered in-app record — the guard, asserted first. in-app+email adds a second record queued pending for the scheduled pass’s drain; mute mints nothing while the audit line answers “why didn’t I get this” in so many words. Each intake triager’s own preference is consulted inside the loop; a rule’s notify is suppressed by its target’s mute but a role label — nobody’s preference — is untouched, and a rule already emailing plus an email preference stays one record. A client-role actor may set her own preferences and not Priya’s, the admin may set anybody’s, and a kind outside the vocabulary is refused naming all three.

findings.title: A week gathered in one place, and a queue the approver can clear

findings.actual: The grid gathers a week across issues without re-filtering: quarter hours sum per day and per issue, a withdrawn entry is excluded, another person’s hours never land, and the id-join matches an entry whose display name went stale. Three submitted weeks make a queue; the panel’s pre-filter — decideProblem per row — excludes the approver’s own week, the remaining two approve as an atomic fold, and the own week asked individually is refused in the rule’s words and stays Submitted.

findings.title: A ticket’s week, as seven cells — summed where hours exist, open where they don’t

findings.actual: Seven cells, Monday through Sunday. Monday carries two entries summed to 3.75, not reported as two; Thursday carries its one entry at 4; Tuesday and Friday are null — open to entry — and Tuesday’s null holds even though the other issue has 8h on that day, because the filter is to this issue.

findings.title: The grid’s cells hold the same three guards the cross-issue grid already proves
findings.expected: An id-joined entry survives a stale display name; a withdrawn entry and another person’s entry are both excluded — restated over `issueWeekCells` so a regression in either function can’t hide behind the other’s passing scenario.
findings.actual: Friday reports 3h — the id-joined stale-name entry, with the withdrawn 5h excluded from the sum. Tuesday stays open: Sam’s 8h on that date never lands in Priya’s cell.

findings.title: Save Week is refused for a frozen week before any cell is looked at
findings.expected: A submitted or approved week short-circuits `gridSaveProblem` on the frozen check alone — the same `isFrozen`/`frozenMessage` the single-entry form already refuses with, so the wording agrees whichever screen somebody sees it on.
findings.actual: With the week Submitted, gridSaveProblem returns the exact frozenMessage text for that status — the same valid cells, with no sheet in play, return null. The frozen check runs and wins before any cell is evaluated.

findings.title: Save Week is refused per cell: over the hour cap, or late without a reason
findings.expected: checkEntry and backdated — the same two checks the single-entry form already runs — are applied to every filled cell; one bad cell blocks the whole save, and a clean set of cells does not.
findings.actual: A clean cell passes with no message. A 15h cell is blocked naming the 12-hour cap — checkEntry’s own words. A cell 10 days late with no reason is blocked; the same cell with a reason attached passes.

findings.title: Every resolved value can say where it came from, and a change can say what it reaches
findings.expected: The sources are the resolvers’ annotated twins — same walk, compared for equality so they cannot fork; the radius names the scopes a change reaches and the ones shielded by their own pin.
findings.actual: The engagement’s own word answers “set here”, the client’s answers “organisation default”, the module inherits the engagement’s and says from whom, and an untouched key answers the shipped default — each source equal to its resolver, so the twins cannot fork. A change at the organisation reaches the client but is shielded from the engagement by its own pin and from the module by the same pin, named; a change at the client reaches only the client.

findings.title: Naming a colleague tells them — once, never the author, and only the newly named
findings.expected: One parser feeds the highlight and the mint; longest name first, word-boundary guarded, unknown tokens left as text; the edit pings only the addition; the mute preference answers in the audit.
findings.actual: The parser takes the longest matching directory name at each @, holds the word boundary (so @Sample is not Sam), and leaves an unknown token as text. A note naming Priya twice pings her once with her directory id on the record; Priya naming herself pings nobody; an edit that keeps her name and adds Sam’s pings only Sam. Her mute preference turns the ping into the audit line that answers why, and a note with no @ mints nothing — the default path untouched.

findings.title: A risk carries its judgement, a decision its outcome — and exposure is never stored
findings.expected: Two shipped types recognised by stable id through the live registry, so a rename keeps the semantics; the judgement bounded 1–5 with null meaning not-yet-judged; the bands turn at their stated boundaries.
findings.actual: Risk and Decision ship by stable id and survive a rename to “Threat” — the word changes, the semantics do not, and the old word stops matching. The bands turn exactly where stated (4 Low, 5 Medium, 14 High, 15 Critical), null propagates as not-yet-judged rather than becoming a number, 0 and 6 are refused in words that name the scale and the way back, and no exposure field exists on the stored record — it is computed from the halves every time. A decision’s outcome rides the ordinary audited edit.

findings.title: A guest sees one client’s marked content, and an unattached seat sees nothing

findings.actual: The OAPIL guest’s view holds OAPIL’s marked record with its ancestor chain and nothing of Rival — not the marked record, not even the nodes; Rival’s guest sees the mirror image. A null scope — a sign-in matching no directory entry, or a client seat nobody attached — empties every table rather than widening to every client, which is the deny-by-default the design demands. The directory refuses an engagement node as a scope in words naming what it must be, and both the scope and the email survive an unrelated rename.

findings.actual: logged: Help · refused: No mailbox covers this address.

findings.title: A three-hop cycle is refused
findings.expected: wouldCreateManagerCycle, driven directly against a hand-built people record — A manages B manages C; proposing C as A's manager would close the loop.
findings.actual: refused

findings.title: An immediate cycle is refused
findings.expected: A manages B; proposing A as B's manager directly would close the loop in one hop.
findings.actual: refused

findings.title: An unrelated manager is allowed — checked as its own case
findings.expected: A check that always refused would also pass RL1/RL2; this is what proves it discriminates.
findings.actual: allowed

findings.title: upsertPerson refuses a manager id that resolves to nobody
findings.expected: The check reads m.people directly, so a typo or a deleted person's stale id is caught the same way.
findings.actual: That manager is not in the directory.

findings.title: upsertPerson refuses a person naming themselves as their own manager
findings.expected: Checked against the resolved id, not op.id, so this also holds for a brand-new person whose op.id is null.
findings.actual: A person cannot be their own manager.

findings.title: upsertPerson refuses a manager id that would create a cycle
findings.expected: Proves the reducer arm actually calls wouldCreateManagerCycle, not a second, possibly-different check.
findings.actual: Priya already reports, directly or indirectly, to this person.

findings.title: deletePerson refuses to delete someone with a direct report, and succeeds once nobody does
findings.expected: Proves deletePerson's new refusal is not permanent — reassigning the report unblocks the exact same delete.
findings.actual: blocked: 1 person reports to Sam. Reassign them first.; then allowed after reassignment

findings.title: directReportsOf returns everybody naming a person as manager, and nobody else
findings.expected: A hand-built people record — A manages B and C, and D reports to nobody. Asking for A's reports must return exactly B and C.
findings.actual: [B, C]

findings.title: directReportsOf returns an empty array for somebody nobody reports to — checked as its own case
findings.expected: A function that returned undefined for "nobody" would still pass PS1 alone; this proves the empty case is a real array, not a missing one.
findings.actual: [] (length 0)

findings.title: updateCareerProfile lets somebody update their own grade without holding config.manage
findings.expected: Self-service is the gate, the same shape setNotificationPref already uses — not a grant.
findings.actual: grade=Senior Consultant

findings.title: updateCareerProfile refuses somebody editing a colleague's career profile without config.manage, naming them
findings.expected: The self check must be false for a mismatched id — this is the security-sensitive case named as the plan's highest risk.
findings.actual: Grade, track and development are the person's own to state. Changing Sam's needs “Configure the platform”.

findings.title: updateCareerProfile lets an administrator edit somebody else's track — the admin exception
findings.expected: Mirrors setNotificationPref's own admin exception.
findings.actual: track=Data

findings.title: updateCareerProfile reuses career()'s absent-versus-cleared rule: an omitted field is untouched, an empty string clears it
findings.expected: The two callers of career() — upsertPerson and updateCareerProfile — must not silently diverge on what "clear" means.
findings.actual: after step1: grade=Consultant developingToward=Practice Lead; after step2: grade=undefined

findings.title: clearing the only recorded career field also clears source — "nothing recorded" is one state, not two
findings.expected: Person.source is documented as three states: stated, default, or absent meaning nothing was ever recorded. career() only ever writes 'stated' or omits the key; it never writes 'default'. Clearing the last career fact back out means nothing is recorded any more, so source must go back to absent too, not stay stuck at 'stated'.
findings.actual: after set: source=stated; after clear: grade=undefined source=undefined

findings.title: visibleRows excludes a matching issue's child issue when the child does not itself pass the filter
findings.expected: This is the bug the profile-screen session found by hand: the count of matches shrank correctly while the tree still showed every child of a match regardless of whether it matched.
findings.actual: visible: [PARENT]

findings.title: visibleRows keeps a matching issue's child issue when the child also passes the filter — checked as its own case
findings.expected: A fix that excluded every child regardless would also pass TV1; this proves it discriminates on the child's own match, not on child-hood itself.
findings.actual: visible: [PARENT, CHILD-HIGH]

findings.title: visibleRows keeps a matching issue's non-issue children (activities, milestones) regardless of the filter
findings.expected: Activities and milestones have no owner/severity/status of their own to fail a filter on — TV1's fix must not have started excluding these too.
findings.actual: visible: [PARENT, ACT]

findings.title: visibleRows hides a genuinely empty structural branch that belongs to a DIFFERENT client than the one selected
findings.expected: Found by inspection, not a user report: Client: OAPIL selected, and Axiocloud's own empty internal projects still rode along above the actual OAPIL results — the "keep an empty branch visible" rule was blind to every filter including client, and a client filter is "show me this client's tree", not "this client's tree plus everyone else's empty leftovers".
findings.actual: visible: [COMPANY, CLIENT-A]

findings.title: visibleRows keeps a genuinely empty structural branch that belongs to the SELECTED client — checked as its own case
findings.expected: A fix that excluded every empty branch regardless of client would also pass TV4; this proves the original "a freshly created empty Project stays visible and selectable" behaviour still holds for the client actually being viewed.
findings.actual: visible: [CLIENT-A, PROJECT-A]

findings.title: visibleRows keeps every empty structural branch, across every client, when no client filter is active
findings.expected: TV4's fix is scoped to filters.client !== 'All' on purpose — this proves the ordinary unfiltered case (Client: All) is untouched.
findings.actual: visible: [CLIENT-B, PROJECT-B]

findings.title: matchingIssue attaches a reply to the one open issue sharing its conversationId
findings.actual: matched OAPIL-1

findings.title: matchingIssue attaches to a matching issue even when it is closed, without the caller reopening it
findings.expected: The design is explicit: a reply on a closed issue adds a note, it does not reopen the issue — a person decides.
findings.actual: matched OAPIL-2

findings.title: matchingIssue picks the most recently active issue when a thread matches more than one
findings.expected: Legacy data from before this shipped, or a thread a person split by hand — the design's own tie-break, never a refusal to pick.
findings.actual: matched OAPIL-NEW

findings.title: matchingIssue ignores a refused message with no issue when matching a later reply on the same thread
findings.expected: A refused message's InboundMail row has no issueId — it named no issue, and cannot become one a later reply matches against.
findings.actual: no match, creates a new issue

findings.title: matchingIssue creates a new issue when there is no conversationId, or nothing matches it
findings.expected: Today's behaviour, unchanged — the intake-form path and any message from a connector that has not been redeployed both hit this.
findings.actual: noId=null, noMatch=null

findings.title: duplicateGroups groups issues sharing client, parent and a Re:/Fwd:-stripped subject, canonical as the most recently active — even one with no InboundMail row at all
findings.expected: The "item master" shape this was built to find: three issues, same thread, filed three times. OAPIL-149 carries no mail row on purpose — the real gap this was rewritten to close.
findings.actual: [{"canonical":"OAPIL-151","duplicates":["OAPIL-149","OAPIL-150"]}]

findings.title: duplicateGroups does not group issues that only share a subject — client and parent must match too
findings.expected: Two unrelated clients both emailing "Weekly status" must not become a group. This is now the only guard against a false positive, since the key no longer requires a shared mailbox.

findings.title: duplicateGroups does not group issues whose subjects merely start alike — the match is on the full normalized subject, not a prefix
findings.expected: "item master" and "item master pricing" are different topics under the same client and parent; nothing about dropping the mailbox from the key should make the subject match looser.

findings.title: normalizeSubject strips only a leading Re:/Fw:/Fwd: run, not one appearing mid-subject
findings.actual: a=true b=true

findings.title: A freshly-emptied score is unscored, not scored at zero
findings.expected: `emptyScores` returns null per dimension, not 0 — `isScored` tells the two apart, and `totalComplexity` still sums a fully-zeroed estimate correctly once every dimension is deliberately set to 0.
findings.actual: emptyScores() is unscored with a total of 0; a record with every dimension explicitly set to 0 is scored, also totalling 0 — the two states are distinguishable even though they sum identically.

findings.title: normaliseScore matches the Axiomate model’s own rounding, not just its endpoints
findings.expected: ROUND((raw/25)×15) at both ends of the raw range and at the design doc’s own worked figure (12→7) — proving the rounding direction, not just that 0 maps to 0 and 25 maps to 15.
findings.actual: normaliseScore(0)=0, normaliseScore(25)=15, normaliseScore(12)=7 — matching the deck's own worked example exactly.

findings.title: Size bands are matched on the normalised score, including the nominal XXL/3XL range
findings.expected: A normalised 3 lands in XS and a normalised 4 lands in S — the boundary the model actually draws — and a normalised 16, unreachable by the real formula, still resolves to XXL because the band is configured, not just documented.
findings.actual: Normalised 3 -> XS, 4 -> S, 15 -> XL (the real ceiling), 16 -> XXL (unreachable by normaliseScore alone, but still a configured band for sizeOverride to land on).

findings.title: deriveEffort reproduces the design doc’s own worked example exactly
findings.expected: Business 4, Technical 5, Integration 0, Testing 2, Data 1 — raw 12, normalised 7, size M — the same arithmetic the design doc quotes from the deck’s slide 13, so a future reader can check this scenario against the deck directly.
findings.actual: rawScore=12 score=7 size=M — matches the deck's slide-13 worked example (raw 12, normalised 7, size M) exactly.

findings.title: The auto-estimator no longer floors an untouched dimension to 1
findings.expected: Text that fires only the "security" rule (business/technical/testing) leaves Data untouched by any content rule — it proposes 0, "no meaningful effort in this dimension," not the old floor of 1 — and the proposal is still scored, since a rule did fire.
findings.actual: scores={"business":3,"technical":2,"integration":1,"testing":3,"data":0}, outcome=scored — Data proposes 0 rather than an assumed 1, Integration still gets its NO_SIGNAL_FLOOR of 1, and the proposal still counts as scored because the security rule actually fired.
